\chapter{Water and Bread}
\label{ch:ar-water-and-bread}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name water and bread in Arabic and say which of the two sits on a regular root.}

Say māʾ with its irregular plural miyāh, then khubz from the clean root kh-b-z.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{ماء} \ar{خبز}]{\ar{ماء}, \ar{خبز} (māʾ, khubz) — water and bread}

\label{lesson:AR-C13-maa-khubz}



\begin{quote}
Two everyday words — and a study in contrasts: one of them is one of Arabic's genuinely \textbf{oddest} common nouns, and the other is about as \textbf{regular} as a word gets.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{ماء} — an old, irregular word}
\textbf{\ar{ماء}} (\emph{māʾ}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{water}.\textquotedblright{} This word is short but \textbf{irregular}: its plural (\textbf{\ar{مياه}}, \emph{miyāh}) and the forms it takes when attached to another noun don't follow Arabic's ordinary noun patterns the way most words do. Words this basic — for water, fire, blood, mouth — are often among the oldest in any language family, and old words wear their irregularities proudly; they were already worn smooth by daily use long before the grammar of the rest of the language settled into its regular patterns.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{خبز} — clean, regular, and freshly made}
\textbf{\ar{خبز}} (\emph{khubz}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{bread}\textquotedblright{} — built cleanly on the root \textbf{\ar{خ}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ز}} (\emph{kh-b-z}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to bake}.\textquotedblright{} Where \emph{māʾ} is a fossil, \emph{khubz} is transparent: the noun for the baked thing, straight from the verb for baking it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}māʾ\textquotedblright{} — water — then \textquotedblleft{}miyāh,\textquotedblright{} its irregular plural
  \item \textquotedblleft{}khubz\textquotedblright{} — bread — from kh-b-z, \textquotedblleft{}to bake\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — one word is a worn-smooth fossil, the other freshly transparent
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What's unusual about \textbf{\ar{ماء}}? (\textbf{It's genuinely irregular} — its plural \emph{miyāh} and attached forms don't follow the ordinary pattern, typical of very old, basic words.) What root is \textbf{\ar{خبز}} built on, and what does that root mean? (\textbf{\ar{خ}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ز}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to bake}.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
